newsitem.title: FINLAND: Nokia targets key role in TV decoders.
newsitem.headline: Nokia targets key role in TV decoders.

text.p: Finnish telecoms major Nokia Oy, which has retained a consumer electronics presence in decoder boxes for digital pay television, said on Wednesday its target was to be among the key players in that growing market.
"We are targeting to be one of the very few key players," Pekka Kuusela, vice-president sales and marketing at Nokia's multimedia network terminals unit, told Reuters by telephone.

He was speaking after Nokia confirmed it would supply its Mediamaster 9601 decoder boxes to new Spanish pay-television operator Via Digital, which plans to launch in September despite a European Union row over Madrid's choice of technology.

Nokia has been sharpening its focus on telecommunications since the early 1990s and last year sold units including television manufacturing, but has kept up multimedia activities focused on Internet and digital video broadcasting protocols.
It says its decoder box is the first of its kind, enabling consumers to change their digital television platform without having to replace the set-top box.

Via Digital plans to rent the boxes at 1,000 pesetas per month. Its preference has been challenged in Brussels by a rival consortium backed by French-pay television operator Canal Plus and its local ally Prisa, pitching for their decoder.
But Kuusela said the order for 50,000 boxes was a firm one, which the company hoped would increase. He declined to detail its value.
"We are looking forward to being a major supplier in Spain," he said, adding that Nokia's decoder had already secured a sizeable chunk of the Italian pay-television market.
There and in Nordic markets, set-top boxes are not sold through the pay-television providers but direct to consumers, Kuusela said.
Nokia won a first decoder breakthrough in Germany and Austria and besides Spain and Italy, Kuusela said it is active in the Middle East and China as main markets.
Nokia's bid for a prime role pits it against rivals like Pace Micro Technology -- one of the suppliers in a recent one-million-box order to a consortium headed by BSkyB.
"We think (ours) is a very competitive product," Kuusela said; a consumer wanting to switch to another pay-television provider platform need change only a card, not the whole box.
Although the market for digital television is yet small, Kuusela was confident digital television would grow to outrank current systems.
"Within a couple of years we will see (this) is inevitable," he said.
